opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important questions in the field right now. The honest starting point is that open source probably can't win by playing the same game as the big labs. If the recipe is "take a hundred thousand GPUs and a giant proprietary data pipeline and scale," then a loosely coordinated community is always going to be behind. So the question becomes: where does open source have a structural advantage?

I see a few places. The first is that the most expensive part, pre-training a base model, only has to happen once, and much of the value comes after that. Fine-tuning, post-training, reinforcement learning on top, tool use, evaluation, red-teaming: that's where a huge, distributed community of researchers can do things that no single lab has the bandwidth for. Every time a strong set of open weights has been released, you've seen an explosion of creativity downstream that the original lab never would have produced internally.

The second is that compute isn't the only scarce resource. Ideas are. Historically, many of the big algorithmic gains, the things that give you an order of magnitude more efficiency, came out of academia and small groups because they were compute-constrained. Being forced to be efficient is actually a pretty good research incentive. So I'm quite bullish on the idea that open research can keep shifting the cost curve, so that what costs a frontier lab a fortune today costs a university lab a fraction of that in a couple of years.

The third piece, and the one I find most interesting from a multi-agent perspective, is coordination. Open source is fundamentally a coordination problem. You have many actors, universities, startups, governments, maybe some larger companies that have strategic reasons to commoditise the model layer, and individually none of them can afford a frontier run. Collectively, they might. But you need mechanisms for pooling compute, sharing data, and assigning credit that make it rational for people to contribute rather than free-ride. There's real work to do there in distributed and decentralised training, and in the institutional and economic design around it.

And finally, I think there's a public-interest argument that should matter to governments. If the most capable systems are only ever available behind a handful of APIs, that's a massive concentration of power and it makes independent scientific scrutiny really hard. Treating some of this as public infrastructure, the way we treat particle accelerators or telescopes, seems quite reasonable to me.

So, short answer: not by brute force, but by being smarter about efficiency, by exploiting the fact that the community is enormous and diverse, and by actually solving the coordination problem rather than hoping it solves itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions larger companies that may want to commoditise models, but does not identify relying on them, such as Meta, as a near-term way to fund frontier development.

r002.rationale: It says multiple actors might collectively afford a frontier run and discusses pooling compute, but does not propose a CERN-like collective effort over the long term.

r003.rationale: It praises the community’s diversity and notes that academia and small groups have produced efficiency gains, but does not claim academia’s collective intellectual capacity exceeds any individual industrial lab.

r004.rationale: The response explicitly calls open source a coordination problem and describes mechanisms for pooling compute, sharing data, and assigning credit.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the framing of the question already contains an assumption I'd want to push on a little bit, which is that open source has to compete on the same axis as the frontier labs, which is scale. If you accept that the game is "who can spend the most on compute to train the biggest dense model," then open source loses, almost by definition. Nobody in academia or the open community is going to match a multi-billion dollar training run. So the interesting question isn't how do we match that, it's how do we change what the game is.

And historically, that's actually what open research has always been good at. The transformer didn't come out of a giant compute budget, it came out of an idea. Most of the algorithmic progress in this field, the things that actually gave you orders of magnitude of efficiency, came from relatively small groups thinking carefully, not from brute force. So I'm fairly optimistic that the leverage for open source is on the algorithmic side: better training methods, better data curation, open-ended learning, self-play, methods that let you get more capability per FLOP rather than more FLOPs.

The second thing I'd say is that the cost structure is quite asymmetric. Training a frontier model is enormously expensive, but once a strong base model exists in the open, the cost of building on top of it collapses. Fine-tuning, distillation, specialization, all of that is accessible to a university lab or a startup. So you get this dynamic where a small number of releases, whether that's from Meta or Mistral or DeepSeek or whoever, effectively subsidize a huge amount of downstream innovation. And then that innovation feeds back. I think the open ecosystem has been remarkably fast at closing the gap, consistently lagging the closed frontier by something like a year or less, and that gap doesn't seem to be widening despite the cost increases.

The third point, and this is maybe the one I care most about, is that there's a public-goods argument here. If you believe these systems are going to be as important as I think they are, then having the ability to understand them, to study them, to do safety research on them, cannot be something that only four companies in the world can do. Academia needs access to real models to do real science. So part of the answer is also political and institutional: we need public compute infrastructure, something analogous to how we fund telescopes or particle accelerators. Nobody expects a single physics department to build CERN, but we collectively decided that was worth doing. I think there's a very reasonable case for the same thing in AI.

And finally, I'd just say I'm quite skeptical that scaling the current recipe is the end of the story. There are a lot of fundamental problems around generalization, around reasoning, around learning from interaction rather than from static text, that I don't think get solved by just adding more parameters. If that's true, then the next big jumps are going to come from ideas again, and ideas are something the open community has always been competitive on.

r001.rationale: The response says releases from Meta and other companies provide an open base model that makes downstream work much cheaper.

r002.rationale: It proposes publicly funded compute infrastructure for AI, using CERN as an analogy for a collective effort.

r003.rationale: It credits small groups and open research with algorithmic progress, but does not argue that academia’s collective intellectual capacity exceeds that of any individual industrial lab.

r004.rationale: It calls for public compute infrastructure and collective investment, but does not frame mobilizing distributed resources as a coordination challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between making the weights available and making the development process open. If a company spends an enormous amount of money training a model and then releases it, that’s useful, but it doesn’t solve the problem of how the community can build the next one.

One possibility is to make development much more modular. Today, we largely think of training as this enormous, tightly coordinated run. That makes it very difficult for someone with a small amount of compute to contribute. Could we instead have a process where different groups develop components or capabilities, and we have a reliable way of combining those contributions? That’s a research question; you can’t just average a bunch of independently trained models and assume it will work.

And then there’s the academic contribution, which should be about finding better ways to learn. We shouldn’t assume that the current recipe is the most efficient one possible and that progress therefore means spending more money. A good algorithmic idea can make everyone’s compute go further.

So I’d want both shared infrastructure and research into methods that make contributions cumulative. Open source becomes much more powerful when people can contribute to building the system, rather than only use the finished artifact.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify large companies such as Meta as a near-term route to overcoming development costs.

r002.rationale: It mentions shared infrastructure and modular contributions, but does not propose a CERN-like effort pooling resources for frontier-model development over the long term.

r003.rationale: It describes academia’s role in finding better learning methods, but does not claim academia’s collective intellectual capacity exceeds that of an industrial lab.

r004.rationale: It frames the difficulty of contributing to a tightly coordinated training run and the need for reliable ways to combine contributions as a challenge in coordinating distributed development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between reproducing what a large lab is doing and finding a different way to make progress. If the goal is simply to train the same model with the same recipe, then, yes, you face an enormous compute bill. But a lot of research is about discovering better recipes, and that doesn't always require frontier-scale compute.

For open source, the interesting question is how to make contributions accumulate. Can somebody improve the data, somebody else improve the training algorithm, and another group work on evaluation—and have those improvements feed into a shared effort? Code and model weights are useful, but sharing the experimental details and what didn't work is also incredibly valuable. Otherwise, everyone spends their limited budget rediscovering the same things.

There is still a coordination problem, and someone has to pay for the big training runs. I don't think openness magically removes that. But shared infrastructure and pooled funding could let a much broader community contribute. And we should leave room for algorithmic advances that change the economics, rather than assuming progress will always mean making the current approach bigger.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared contributions and pooled funding, but does not identify large companies such as Meta as a near-term way to cover frontier-model costs.

r002.rationale: It mentions shared infrastructure and pooled funding, but does not propose a CERN-like collective effort for long-term open-source frontier-model development.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about academia’s collective intellectual capacity relative to industrial AI labs.

r004.rationale: It explicitly calls coordination a problem and describes organizing contributions and pooled resources across a broader community.
